title: Granny square size and gauge
subtitle: How yarn weight and hook size control the finished size of a granny square
excerpt: The same granny square pattern produces finished squares anywhere from 4 cm to 20 cm across depending on the yarn weight and hook size used. Understanding this relationship lets you choose the right combination for a project rather than being surprised by a square that comes out the wrong size.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework, 1886, Project Gutenberg #20776. Weldon's Practical Crochet, 1880s to 1900s, Internet Archive. Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing).

glossaryTerms.definition: The finished size of a granny square after the stated number of rounds, worked at a specific yarn weight and hook size. Varies significantly with changes in yarn weight or hook.
The finished dimensions of one granny square in a project. All squares in the same project should match to a single set to produce a flat, regular joined fabric.

content.text: Granny square gauge

is the finished size of one square, measured across the flat side from centre to edge. The same 4-round granny square pattern gives you a 5 cm square in 2-ply lace-weight thread at a 1.5 mm hook and a 12 cm square in aran-weight yarn at a 5.0 mm hook. The stitch count is identical; only the yarn weight and hook change.

This matters most when planning blankets and throws, where you might need 100 or 200 squares. A square that measures 1 cm larger than expected produces a blanket that is 10 cm wider per 10 squares. Always work a test square and measure it before committing to the full project quantity.
What you need

items.name: Project yarn
items.note: The exact yarn you plan to use for the project, not a substitute.

items.name: Hook at the label-recommended size and one size up and one down
Blocking mat and pins
items.note: Optional but useful for measuring accurate post-block dimensions.

content.text: Reference sizes for common yarn weights
A standard 4-round granny square gives approximately these sizes in a typical sample. Your yarn and tension will differ; use this as a starting point only.
Lace weight (1.5 mm hook): approximately 5 to 6 cm
Fingering / 4-ply (2.5 mm hook): approximately 7 to 8 cm
DK (4.0 mm hook): approximately 9 to 11 cm
Aran (5.0 mm hook): approximately 11 to 13 cm
Chunky (6.0 mm hook): approximately 13 to 15 cm
Calculating the number of squares for a blanket
Work one test square. Block it and measure.
Divide the finished blanket width by the
square set
to find the number of squares per row.
Divide the finished blanket length by the square set to find the number of rows of squares.
Multiply rows by columns to find total squares needed. Add 5 to 10% for waste and rejected squares.
Common problems

items.symptom: Squares from different yarn balls are not the same size
items.cause: Different dye lots have slightly different spun diameters, causing gauge variation.
items.fix: Work a test square from each new ball of yarn before adding it to the project. If the size difference is 0.5 cm or more, consider separating the squares from different lots into different rows or blocks.

items.symptom: Squares worked later in the project are measurably different from early squares
items.cause: Tension changes with practice or fatigue.
items.fix: Measure every 10th square and adjust hook size if the trend is consistent. It is normal to work slightly looser as you relax into a project.

items.symptom: Joined squares are lying flat but the blanket is not square
items.cause: Individual squares are not square, having grown more in one direction than the other.
items.fix: Block each individual square to a measured square template before joining. A piece of cardboard cut to the target size works as a blocking template.

content.text: What to try next

Work one 4-round granny square in three different yarn weights using the same basic pattern: lace weight, DK, and aran. Block all three and compare the finished sizes. This demonstration makes the yarn-weight-to-size relationship concrete and informs every future project that uses modular squares.
